results.result: Gzma-/- mice have a mixed C57BL/6J and C57BL/6N genetic background (~60% 6N, ~40% 6J) and retain the full-length Nnt gene, whereas C57BL/6J mice have a truncated Nnt gene with a 5-exon deletion. This mixed background arose because the BL/6-III ES cells used to generate Gzma-/- mice were derived from C57BL/6N mice, which were frequently used for knockout generation due to better germline transmission rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C41 are strongly supported by whole-genome sequencing data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), RNA-Seq Sashimi plots (Figure 3d), RT-PCR (Figure 3e), and WGS alignment to C3H/HeJ genome (Figure 3c). Claims C3, C16 are supported by prior literature and confirmed by current data. Claims C14, C15, C42, C43 are supported by citations and logical inference from the WGS data showing the mixed background.

results.result: CHIKV-induced foot swelling was substantially ameliorated in Gzma-/- mice compared to 6J mice; however, this phenotype was due to the presence of Nnt and the C57BL/6N background rather than loss of GZMA expression. This was demonstrated by showing that 6N mice (with intact Nnt) also showed reduced foot swelling, while GzmaS211A mice (enzymatically inactive GZMA on pure 6J background) showed no reduction in foot swelling compared to 6J mice. Viremia was not significantly different across strains.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C24, C25, C26 are directly supported by foot swelling measurements in Figure 1a and viremia data in Figure 1b with appropriate statistical analysis (p<0.002 for multiple days). Claim C5 is supported by the convergent evidence from multiple mouse strains showing that genetic background, not GZMA loss, drives the phenotype. The experimental design appropriately controls for confounding variables.

results.result: GzmaS211A mice were generated by CRISPR on a C57BL/6J background with the reactive site serine changed to alanine, resulting in loss of enzyme activity. GZMA expression in resting splenic NK cells was comparable between GzmaS211A and 6J mice. Viral titers in feet after CHIKV infection were not significantly different between GzmaS211A and 6J mice, indicating that enzymatically active GZMA has no significant antiviral activity against CHIKV.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C33 are supported by CRISPR generation data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a-c), BLT assays confirming loss of enzyme activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d), and FACS analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e). Claims C34, C35, C36 are supported by viral titer data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f) and consistent with prior work (Wilson et al., 2017). The inference that GZMA lacks antiviral activity is appropriately drawn from the lack of difference in viral titers.

results.result: 6N∆Nnt8-12 mice were generated by CRISPR to delete Nnt exons 8-12 from 6N mice, creating the same deletion present in 6J mice. After CHIKV infection, foot swelling in 6N∆Nnt8-12 mice was significantly higher than in 6N mice and comparable to 6J mice, demonstrating that the absence of functional Nnt can by itself promote overt foot swelling. The increased swelling was due primarily to increased edema rather than cellular infiltrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are supported by CRISPR generation data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and foot swelling measurements (Figure 4a) with appropriate statistical analysis (p values 0.0005-0.042 on days 2-7). Claims C48-C49 represent appropriate inferences from the data. Claims C50-C51 are supported by H&E staining (Figure 4c-d) and immunohistochemistry (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The experimental design provides strong causal evidence for Nnt's role.

results.result: MitoTEMPO treatment (days 3-8 post infection) significantly ameliorated peak foot swelling in CHIKV-infected 6J mice without affecting viremia. The treatment significantly reduced both cellular infiltrate and edema in infected feet. MitoTEMPO treatment in 6J mice and an intact Nnt gene in 6N mice provided overlapping anti-inflammatory activities, as demonstrated by IPA USR analysis showing 10 cytokine USRs downregulated in both comparisons.
results.evaluation: Claims C54, C56, C57 are strongly supported by foot swelling data (Figure 5a, p<0.001 on days 6-8), H&E staining with quantitation (Figure 5c-d, p=0.004 for infiltrate; Figure 5e-f, p=0.008 for edema). Claim C55 is supported by viremia data (Figure 5b). Claim C58 is supported by IPA USR analysis (Figure 4e) showing mechanistic overlap. The experimental design appropriately tests the hypothesis that MitoTEMPO compensates for Nnt deficiency.

results.result: Poly(I:C) injection i.v. into 6J mice induced rapid GZMA release, reaching mean peak serum levels of ~20 ng/ml after 2 hours, then dropping to baseline by 24 hours. Type I IFNs augment but are not required for GZMA release, as Ifnar-/- mice showed blunted but not absent GZMA elevation. The active site mutation in GzmaS211A does not affect GZMA production, secretion, or stability. No serum GZMB was detected after poly(I:C) treatment, consistent with GZMB and perforin appearing only after ~24 hours of stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61, C64, C66 are directly supported by ELISA data (Figure 6a, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) with appropriate statistical analysis (p=0.004 for Ifnar-/- comparison). Claims C62-C63, C65 represent appropriate inferences from the data. Claims C67-C68 are supported by prior literature (Fehniger et al., 2007). The experimental design appropriately characterizes the kinetics and requirements for GZMA secretion.

results.result: RNA-Seq of GzmaS211A vs 6J feet 6 hours after poly(I:C) injection identified 199 DEGs, with 100 downregulated in GzmaS211A mice. The top annotations for downregulated DEGs were associated with negative regulation of protease activity and cell signaling, supporting that GZMA is proteolytically active in vivo and mediates cell signaling. IPA analysis identified downregulation of inflammation and leukocyte activation signatures, with STAT6, STAT3, NFATC2, JUN, NFKB1, and STAT1 as dominant downregulated transcription factor signatures.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71, C74-C75 are directly supported by RNA-Seq data (Supplementary file 6b), Cytoscape analysis (Figure 6b, Table 1), and IPA analysis (Figure 6b, Figure 6—figure supplement 4a). Claims C72-C73 represent appropriate inferences from the data showing negative regulation of protease activity and cell signaling. The experimental design comparing enzymatically active vs inactive GZMA on the same genetic background provides strong evidence for GZMA's proteolytic activity in vivo.

results.result: k-mer mining of the NCBI Sequence Read Archive revealed that ~27% of Run Accessions (1008 of 3744) and ~38% of BioProjects listing C57BL/6J as the mouse strain had Nnt sequencing reads inconsistent with a C57BL/6J genetic background (reads for both Nnt exons 2 and 9, indicating full-length Nnt). This suggests that mouse strain listing errors or inadequate backcrossing to 6J are common for SRA RNA-Seq submissions.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9 are supported by k-mer mining analysis (Supplementary file 7a-c) with validation by BLAST alignments (Supplementary file 7d, Figure 8—figure supplement 1b). The methodology is described in detail (Figure 8—figure supplement 1a) and uses conservative criteria (exact match for 'C57BL/6J', file size filters, no mismatches for 31-mer k-mers, read count >10). Claim C105 is an appropriate inference from the high percentage of inconsistent entries. The analysis provides strong evidence for widespread misreporting or mixed backgrounds.

results.result: RNA-Seq of CHIKV-infected feet (day 6) showed 1073 DEGs between Gzma-/- and 6J mice. IPA analysis showed dominant annotations associated with decreased cell movement (leukocyte migration), and a series of pro-inflammatory cytokine upstream regulators were downregulated in Gzma-/- mice. These findings are consistent with prior immunohistochemistry data showing significantly reduced T cell and NK cells in arthritic infiltrates in Gzma-/- mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29 are directly supported by RNA-Seq data (Supplementary file 2a-b) and IPA analysis (Figure 2a-b, Supplementary file 2c-e) with appropriate statistical filtering (q<0.01). Claim C30 is supported by prior work (Wilson et al., 2017). The convergent evidence from transcriptomics and immunohistochemistry strengthens the conclusions about reduced inflammation in Gzma-/- mice.

results.result: The Nnt gene is located ~6.2 megabases from the Gzma gene on mouse chromosome 13, requiring >30 backcrosses to segregate these loci. This close genetic linkage means that Gzma-/-/Gzmb-/- double-knockout mice would also very likely have full-length Nnt.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C19 are supported by genetic mapping data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and citation (Silver, 2008). The calculation of >30 backcrosses required is based on established genetic distance principles. Claim C87 is an appropriate inference from the genetic linkage data. This provides important context for interpreting studies using these mouse strains.

results.result: NNT is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane and catalyzes the conversion of NADH plus NADP+ to NAD+ plus NADPH, thereby sustaining mitochondrial antioxidant capacity through generation of NADPH. Loss of active NNT in 6J mice is associated with reduced ability to detoxify reactive oxygen species via the glutathione and thioredoxin pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C23 are well-established biochemical facts supported by multiple prior citations (Rydström, 2006; Ward et al., 2020; McCambridge et al., 2019; Meimaridou et al., 2018; Ronchi et al., 2013). These claims provide essential background for understanding the functional consequences of Nnt deletion in 6J mice and the rationale for the MitoTEMPO experiments.

results.result: Serpinb6b inhibited CHIKV foot swelling in GzmaS211A mice (where GZMA is enzymatically inactive), arguing that Serpinb6b can inhibit other unknown proteases involved in promoting arthritic inflammation. This is supported by the broad inhibitory activity of the human orthologue, SerpinB6.
results.evaluation: Claim C38 is supported by experimental data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g). Claims C39-C40 represent appropriate inferences supported by prior literature (Strik et al., 2004). This finding is important because it challenges the interpretation of prior studies using Serpinb6b as a specific GZMA inhibitor and suggests off-target effects.

results.result: STAT3 and NF-κB have been shown to be activated in macrophages by recombinant GZMA in vitro, and monocytes/macrophages are reported as targets for GZMA activity in various settings. GSEA identified gene sets associated with activated monocytes that were significantly enriched in the downregulated genes for GzmaS211A + polyIC vs. 6J + polyIC.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C77 are supported by multiple prior citations (Santiago et al., 2020; Garzón-Tituaña et al., 2021; Metkar et al., 2008; Santiago et al., 2017; Spencer et al., 2013; Uranga et al., 2016). Claim C78 is supported by GSEA analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 4b). This provides mechanistic insight into GZMA's cellular targets and is consistent with the transcription factor signatures identified.

results.result: Only 4 DEGs were identified in the spleen of poly(I:C)-treated GzmaS211A vs. 6J mice, with Mid1 (involved in controlling granule exocytosis) as the only significantly upregulated DEG. GSEA showed that DEGs identified in feet were not enriched in spleen, arguing that GZMA's activity in the periphery is not significantly recapitulated in spleen.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 are supported by RNA-Seq data (Supplementary file 6d). Claim C81 is supported by prior literature (Boding et al., 2014; Boding et al., 2015). Claim C82 is supported by GSEA analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) and represents an appropriate inference. This demonstrates tissue-specific effects of circulating GZMA.

results.result: Serum GZMA levels during CHIKV infection (~0.2 and ~0.075 ng/ml) were substantially lower than after poly(I:C) treatment (~20 ng/ml). Only small overlaps (27 genes for day 2, 20 genes for day 7) were evident between DEGs upregulated during CHIKV infection and DEGs upregulated by proteolytically active GZMA. The magnitude of cytokine USR effects was much smaller for poly(I:C) treatment compared to CHIKV infection, indicating that GZMA plays only a minor role in stimulating immune and inflammation pathways during CHIKV viremia and arthritis.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 are supported by ELISA data (Figure 7c), Venn diagram analysis (Figure 7c, Supplementary file 6i), and USR comparison (Figure 7d). Claim C86 is an appropriate inference from the convergent evidence showing low GZMA levels, small gene overlap, and smaller magnitude of effects during CHIKV infection. This reconciles the apparent contradiction between Gzma-/- and GzmaS211A phenotypes.

results.result: GZMA is a serine protease secreted by cytotoxic lymphocytes including NK cells, NKT cells, and CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C13 are well-established facts supported by multiple prior citations (Fehniger et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2019; Gordy et al., 2011; Suhrbier et al., 1991) and confirmed by experiments in this study showing NK cells as the likely source of GZMA after poly(I:C) treatment. This provides essential background information.

results.result: Injection of proteolytically active, but not proteolytically inactive, recombinant mouse GZMA induced inflammatory foot swelling, demonstrating that GZMA's protease activity can drive pro-inflammatory responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 are supported by prior work (Schanoski et al., 2019). This provides important context for interpreting the current results and supports the rationale for generating the GzmaS211A mice to test the role of GZMA's proteolytic activity.

results.result: Another Gzma-/- mouse generated using 129/SvJ ES cells would likely have the same Nnt issue as 129/SvJ mice have a full-length Nnt gene.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89 are supported by citation (Shresta et al., 1997) and established knowledge about 129/SvJ mice having full-length Nnt. This is an appropriate inference that extends the implications of the findings to other Gzma-/- mouse lines.

results.result: The 6J genome has a 12-nucleotide insertion at the Nnt exon 8-12 deletion junction. These 12 nucleotides are absent in other 6N WGS data, indicating this is not unique to Gzma-/- mice. This insertion may have accompanied deletion of Nnt exons 8-12 during the generation of 6J mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 are supported by WGS alignment data (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 3a). Claim C92 is speculative but supported by the data and citation (Fontaine and Davis, 2016). This provides interesting mechanistic insight into the origin of the Nnt deletion in 6J mice, though it is not central to the main conclusions.

results.result: Gzmb-/- mice are missing Nnt exons 8-12, consistent with a 6J background.
results.evaluation: Claim C93 is supported by RT-PCR data (Figure 3e). This demonstrates that the Nnt issue is not unique to Gzma-/- mice and extends to other granzyme knockout lines, broadening the implications of the findings.

results.result: Pronounced foot swelling in all comparisons was associated with upregulation of TNF, IFNG, and IL-6 USRs, consistent with the arthritis literature. IL-13 was a consistently upregulated USR and is associated with resolution of arthritic inflammation, with peak CHIKV arthritis in 6J mice associated with a significant resolution phase signature.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 are supported by IPA USR analysis (Figure 4e) and multiple prior citations (Kato, 2020; Ma and Xu, 2013; Ogata et al., 2019; Suhrbier, 2019; Schett, 2019; Prow et al., 2019). This provides mechanistic context for the inflammatory responses observed across different experimental conditions.

results.result: MitoTEMPO has been widely used as an experimental antioxidant treatment to scavenge mitochondrial ROS in various disease settings, with >300 papers using MitoTEMPO in 6J mice. However, MitoTEMPO treatment may simply be correcting the Nnt defect in 6J mice by scavenging excess mitochondrial ROS. Unfortunately, antioxidants have not shown clear benefits in human clinical trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C98, C100-C101 are supported by multiple prior citations and PubMed literature search. Claim C99 is speculative but represents a reasonable interpretation supported by citation (Ward et al., 2020) and the mechanistic understanding of NNT and MitoTEMPO function. This raises important questions about the translational relevance of MitoTEMPO studies in 6J mice.

results.result: The Jackson Laboratory generated the 6J inbred mouse strain in the 1920s-1930s, and it is the most frequently used mouse strain in biomedical research. Although differences in the Nnt gene have previously been reported as underappreciated in metabolism research, the data argue that this issue extends to other areas of research.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103 are established historical facts. Claim C104 is supported by multiple prior citations (Fontaine and Davis, 2016; Bourdi et al., 2011; Leskov et al., 2017; McCambridge et al., 2019; and many others) and the current findings. This provides important context for the broader implications of the study.

results.result: Nnt has been reported to affect redox regulation and activation in macrophages. An intact Nnt gene may conceivably reduce cross-presentation and CD8 T cell responses.
results.evaluation: Claim C106 is supported by prior citations (Ripoll et al., 2012; Salerno et al., 2019). Claims C107-C108 are explicitly speculative ('conceivably') and supported only by citations (Dingjan et al., 2016; Nalle et al., 2020; Oberkampf et al., 2018) without direct experimental validation in this study. These represent hypotheses that would require additional experiments to confirm.

results.result: Circulating GZMA in humans is proteolytically active. Humans, nonhuman primates, and mice have elevated serum GZMA levels after infection with CHIKV and other RNA viruses, with NK cells identified as the likely source.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C112 are supported by prior work (Spaeny-Dekking et al., 1998; Schanoski et al., 2019; Wilson et al., 2017). This provides important context for the physiological relevance of the findings and supports the rationale for using poly(I:C) to induce GZMA secretion.

results.result: Resting NK cells constitutively contain abundant levels of GZMA protein, which is stored in granules as a mature protease, with the low pH of the granule preventing premature proteolytic activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C115 are well-established facts supported by prior citations (Fehniger et al., 2007; Stewart et al., 2012). This provides essential background for understanding GZMA biology and the rapid release observed after poly(I:C) treatment.

results.result: Poly(I:C) can mimic aspects of innate responses to RNA viruses and is known to activate NK cells. Type I interferons are rapidly induced by poly(I:C), and NK cells express the type I IFN receptor and can respond to type I IFNs.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C119 are well-established facts supported by multiple prior citations (Prow et al., 2017; Djeu et al., 1979; Fehniger et al., 2007; Miyake et al., 2009; Ngoi et al., 2008; Dempoya et al., 2012; Santiago-Raber et al., 2003; Madera et al., 2016; Mizutani et al., 2012). This provides essential background for the rationale of using poly(I:C) to study GZMA function.

results.result: Circulating proteolytically active GZMA promotes immune-stimulating and pro-inflammatory signatures.
results.evaluation: Claim C7 is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of GzmaS211A vs 6J mice after poly(I:C) injection showing downregulation of inflammation and leukocyte activation signatures in GzmaS211A mice (Figure 6b, Supplementary file 6f). This is a key finding that provides the first clear evidence for GZMA's pro-inflammatory activity free from genetic background confounds.
